paragraphs.heading: The group 1 family
paragraphs.text: The alkali metals are six elements: lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium and francium. Together with hydrogen they make up group 1, which sits in the s-block of the periodic table. Each one keeps its outermost electron in an s-orbital, and that shared arrangement gives them very similar properties. They are also called the lithium family, after the element at the top.

paragraphs.heading: Soft, shiny and reactive
paragraphs.text: At ordinary temperature and pressure they are shiny, soft metals that react very easily. They readily give up their outer electron and become cations, particles with a charge of +1. A knife cuts them easily, and the bright fresh surface quickly dulls as moisture and oxygen in the air attack it. So they are stored under oil, and in nature they turn up only in salts, never as pure metal. All of them react with water, the heavier ones more violently, and caesium is the most reactive of all metals.

paragraphs.heading: Where they are found
paragraphs.text: In nature these metals exist as compounds. Sodium is the most plentiful, then potassium, lithium, rubidium and caesium. Francium is very rare because it is extremely radioactive, and it shows up only in minute traces partway along some natural decay chains. Experiments to make element 119, the likely next member, have all failed, and it might not behave as an alkali metal anyway.

paragraphs.heading: Uses in daily life
paragraphs.text: Most alkali metals have many uses. Rubidium and caesium are used in atomic clocks, and caesium clocks are the basis of the second. Sodium-vapour lamps give off light very efficiently, and table salt, sodium chloride, has been in use since antiquity. Lithium serves as a psychiatric drug and as the anode in lithium batteries. Sodium, potassium and possibly lithium are essential to the body, where they act as electrolytes.

paragraphs.heading: Pulling metals from salts
paragraphs.text: In 1807, in England, Humphry Davy became the first to isolate pure potassium. He used electrolysis of molten caustic potash, powered by the newly invented voltaic pile. Earlier tries on the salt dissolved in water had failed because potassium reacts so fiercely. Potassium was the first metal isolated by electrolysis, and later that year Davy drew sodium from caustic soda in a similar way.

paragraphs.heading: Names from stone and colour
paragraphs.text: Lithium was detected in 1817 by Johan August Arfwedson while he was analysing petalite ore. Berzelius named the new material after the Greek word lithos, meaning stone, because it came from a solid mineral, and called the metal lithium. Rubidium and caesium were the first elements found with the spectroscope, which Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff invented in 1859. Their names come from the strongest lines in their light: red for rubidium, from Latin rubidus, and sky-blue for caesium, from caesius.
